newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 9.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- TALK OF RETURN TO ERM HITS POUND

Reports of a Labour Government plan to take the currency back into the European exchange rate mechanism at a rate of 2.50 marks, led to the pound being hit by a wave of selling. The currency tumbled in Far Eastern markets overnight and remained under pressure in European trading. The Treasury dismissed the reports which were put out by a news agency and quoted by a senior, though unnamed, Labour source.
-- ARTHUR ANDERSEN TO NET KWIK SAVE FEE OF 20 MILLION STG
Arthur Andersen, the management consultant, is to receive 20 million stg from Kwik Save for its work advising the discount food retailer during its proposed three-year recovery plan.

Derek Pretty, finance director, disclosed that the company would pay Arthur Andersen 10 million stg this year. Kwik Save announced that interim profits had slipped to 40.7 million stg, saying sales were declining faster than City expectations.
-- BYATT CALLS FOR WATER CHARGES SHAKE-UP

Ian Byatt, the industry regulator, has proposed sweeping changes in the way water charges are fixed, with more incentives to encourage customers to switch to meters and seasonal variations in domestic tariffs. Byatt wants a maximum 27 stg differential between bills for metered and unmetered customers and believes large industrial companies should be taken out of the price net without domestic customers being affected.
THE TIMES
-- BTR SHARES SLUMP AFTER SECOND PROFIT WARNING
BTR shares fell 14 percent after the company issued its second profits warning within a year. The price drop wiped 1.6 billion stg off the value of Britain's biggest conglomerate.
Chief executive Ian Strachan blames the poor performance on the strong pound and weaker than expected markets in Germany and Australia. The warning prompted heavy selling of the shares.
-- LABOUR AIMS FOR BILLIONS IN PFI PROJECTS

The Labour Government has announced that it will streamline the workings of the Private Finance Initiative (PFI) by removing a key obstacle to having billions of stg of privately funded public sector projects approved rapidly. The Treasury will end the universal testing of all PFI schemes. The move has been welcomed by business. Also, the private sector has announced it will led a review of the whole PFI process, to be completed within six weeks.
-- BCCI FRAUD REAPS GOKAL RECORD 14 YEARS IN JAIL

Abbas Gokal, former chairman of the Gulf Group, has been jailed for 14 years by the Old Bailey in London. He siphoned $1.2 billion from the Bank of Credit and Commerce International through a number of offshore companies, threatening ruin for thousands of bank depositors. He became Britain's biggest fraudster. Mr Justice Buxton said his actions had threatened the integrity of the entire international banking system.
THE GUARDIAN
-- PENSION FUNDS SET TO FIGHT TAX GRAB

Chancellor Gordon Brown is facing a row in his attempt to boost government income, because of the threat to the pensions industry's tax benefits. The industry is fending off an attack on its tax perks amid fears that the Treasury aims to raise as much as eight billion stg by changing the company tax system.
Director-general of the National Association of Pension Funds, Ann Robinson, said the Government would be making a mistake if it hit pension perks.
-- SALES SURGED AS TORIES SLUMPED
According to the Confederation of British Industry, a surge in consumer confidence last month boosted high street spending.

Retail sales volumes showed the highest annual rate of increase since November 1996 and the growth is expected to continue this month. The City seized on the consumer boom as justification over the Chancellor's decision to raise base rates 0.25 percent.
However, others claim this is further evidence of the widening gap between the services and manufacturing sector.
-- PRESCOTT ORDERS RAIL CURBS AS SWT ESCAPES

Deputy prime minister John Prescott has ordered a tightening of the law governing private rail companies after withdrawing a threatened fine of one million stg against South West Trains. The move comes after Prescott and Gavin Strang, the Transport Secretary, were told by John O'Brien, the rail franchising director, that SWT had improved its service to commuters since getting rid of 71 drivers. Labour are not happy that the Railways Act prevented O'Brien from imposing the fine.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BT TO GET EARLY RELEASE FROM BAR ON BROADCAST TV

The Government is in negotiations with British Telecom aimed at allowing the group to move into entertainment broadcasting, competing with the cable television industry. This could end the ban on BT broadcasting entertainment across its telephone network. National Heritage Secretary Chris Smith has indicated that Labour would fulfil the promise it made two years ago. He expects BT to fulfil its pledge to connect, for free, schools, hospitals and libraries to the information highway.
-- HOLLICK INVESTS 120 MLN STG IN BID FOR DIGITAL TERRESTRIAL LICENCE

United News & Media is to join Digital Television Network, one of two bidders for the licence to run digital terrestrial television, with an investment of 120 million stg over four years. United has been part of DTN's programming submission to the Independent Television Commission but has not been financially involved. The ITC is expected to award the licences by early next month.
-- CWC SET TO CUT 500 JOBS IN INITIAL OVERHAUL

Cable & Wireless Communications is about to cut hundreds of managerial jobs as it merges the administrative operations of the four companies which joined to form the new venture. One source claims that the process was likely to result in a total of 200 job cuts because there were more applications than jobs available. Chief executive Graham Wallace said the selection process for the cuts had been fair and above board.
